newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Islamic Jihad threat puts Israel on alert.
newsitem.headline: Islamic Jihad threat puts Israel on alert.

text.p: Israeli police went on high alert, intensifying security checks on the roads and at shopping malls on Sunday, for fear of a suicide attack by Islamic Jihad militants on a key anniversary.
"It's in the context of the possibility of Islamic Jihad committing an attack to mark a year since the death of Fathi Shqaqi, the organisation's leader," Police Chief Assaf Hefetz told army radio
"Security forces take this threat very seriously and so this preparedness," he said. "We don't know the kind of attack exactly but it could be an explosion, suicide, shots."
Islamic Jihad, responsible for suicide attacks in Israel, accuses the Jewish state of killing Shqaqi, gunned down on October 26, 1995, in Malta. His assassins were never caught.
Security sources said a car bomb might already have been smuggled into Israel and its operators could be waiting for a green light to carry out the attack.
Public Security Minister Avigdor Kahalani told army radio the expected target was in one of the Israeli cities -- Jerusalem, Tel Aviv or Haifa.

Right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, sounding like the Nobel peace laureate Shimon Peres he ousted in May, accused guerrillas of trying to torpedo peace moves. He said "external elements" were behind them.

Roadblocks on the Jerusalem-Tel Aviv highway caused commuters to arrive at work more than two hours late. The manager of Jerusalem's central bus station said the checkpoints prompted many would-be travellers to stay home.
At Jerusalem's main shopping mall, border police inspected cars. A sniffer dog was used to search for explosives. Large paramilitary forces patrolled the mall itself.
Palestinian police in the Gaza Strip last month arrested dozens of Islamic Jihad members to pre-empt any attacks by the movement, a PLO security official said.

Islamic Jihad and Hamas leaders have been in jail since suicide bombings in February and March, responsibility for which was claimed by Hamas, the other leading Islamic resistance group in Palestinian areas.
Israel on October 23 sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip, barring Palestinians from going to work in the Jewish state, for fear of attacks. That closure remains in place.
In the West Bank city of Hebron, Jewish settlers hurled petrol bombs at a Palestinian house on Sunday, setting it ablaze and injuring five people, one critically, family members said.
Israeli police said they were investigating the report.
Under an interim peace deal, Hebron was to be handed over to the PLO in March, but the move was delayed for security reasons.
The PLO and Israel have failed to reach agreement on the handover of the city, a flashpoint of violence where 400 settlers live and study among more than 100,000 Palestinians.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind, on a one-day Middle East trip, tried to nudge Israeli and Palestinian peacemakers closer to an accord on Hebron.

"There is a real prospect for agreement on Hebron over the near future but that will require both sides to address these matters in an inspired way that recognises the great prizes to be won," Rifkind told reporters.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said Egypt was trying to close a deal between the PLO and Israel. But Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy blamed Arafat for the delay.
Israel's Trade and Industry Minister Natan Sharansky urged an information campaign to prepare the public for the possibility of war in light of heightened tensions with Syria.
